On June 18, 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) voted unanimously to expedite the process for connecting rapidly growing, energy-intensive AI data centers to the U.S. electric transmission grid. Prompted by Energy Secretary Chris Wright to enhance competitiveness with China in AI, FERC directed six regional grid operators to ensure timely and efficient access to power for massive data centers—some consuming more electricity than small cities. While clean energy advocates and state authorities voiced concerns about losing oversight and environmental impact, FERC emphasized that states will retain control over retail electricity rates and terms.

The order mandates that data centers bear the full cost of necessary grid upgrades but aims to address significant energy supply constraints. The Edison Electric Institute supported the plan, citing its alignment with current state and regional efforts. However, with over 4,000 data centers already in operation and 3,000 more planned, local opposition and logistical challenges persist. FERC’s directive requires grid operators to report within 30-60 days on plans to accommodate the rising demand. This move highlights the urgency of adapting outdated grid systems to meet AI-driven electricity needs, which could triple by 2035.

items.snippet: On June 18, 2026, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) approved a new framework proposed by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) to manage the rising electricity demand from data centers and other large-scale consumers. This initiative, known as the "Batch Zero" process, consolidates qualified projects with demands of at least 75 megawatts into a single study. The approach allows ERCOT to assess future electricity needs, allocate grid capacity efficiently, and determine necessary transmission upgrades. Currently, ERCOT is evaluating over 438,000 MW in large-load requests, with approximately 89% originating from data centers. As U.S. power consumption reached record highs in 2025 and is projected to grow further, this framework addresses the increased strain on the electrical grid, especially as certain data centers rival entire cities in energy use. ERCOT plans to inform Batch Zero participants of their classifications by August 2026 and release a finalized transmission plan in fall 2027. Applications for the subsequent wave, Batch 1, are scheduled to begin in summer 2027.

Anthropic plans broader trusted access to Mythos 5 due to its unmatched cybersecurity abilities. The naming aligns with Anthropic’s thematic tradition, with "Fable" being etymologically connected to "Mythos."

The launch coincides with Anthropic filing for an IPO and follows a similar filing by rival OpenAI. The U.S. government recently enacted a voluntary disclosure policy for AI companies to share access to frontier models pre-release, aiming to mitigate fears of advanced AI exposing critical software vulnerabilities.

Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5, a powerful "Mythos-class" AI model, while embedding strict safeguards to prevent misuse, especially in cybersecurity, biology, and chemistry. These restrictions defer sensitive queries to its Opus 4.8 model. Available immediately to Pro, Max, team, and enterprise subscribers, Fable 5 will require usage credits from June 23 unless capacity allows an extension. The model is described as state-of-the-art in AI, excelling in software engineering, scientific tasks, and complex reasoning, with companies like Stripe and IMC reporting significant performance boosts.

Fable 5 is a safeguarded version of Claude Mythos 5—identical in core architecture but without some restrictions—which is being selectively shared with cybersecurity experts through Project Glasswing. Anthropic plans broader trusted access to Mythos 5 due to its unmatched cybersecurity abilities. The naming aligns with Anthropic’s thematic tradition, with "Fable" being etymologically connected to "Mythos."

The launch coincides with Anthropic filing for an IPO and follows a similar filing by rival OpenAI. The U.S. government recently enacted a voluntary disclosure policy for AI companies to share access to frontier models pre-release, aiming to mitigate fears of advanced AI exposing critical software vulnerabilities.

supporting_websites.snippet:
Anthropic has launched Claude Fable 5, a new AI model built on the same foundation as the previously restricted Claude Mythos 5, a system originally deemed too powerful for public release due to its advanced cybersecurity capabilities. While Mythos 5 was made available only to select organizations via Project Glasswing—a U.S. government-collaborated initiative aimed at strengthening cyberdefense—Claude Fable 5 is accessible to the general public. However, it includes built-in guardrails that automatically restrict access to sensitive functionalities related to cybersecurity, biology, chemistry, and model extraction. In cases where those capabilities are requested, a less powerful model is substituted. These safeguards reportedly work in 95% of user sessions, making the restrictions largely invisible to most users.

Claude Fable 5 exemplifies a new middle-ground strategy for AI deployment: public release with selective feature disablement. This approach contrasts with prior industry practices that typically involved either full model releases with safety filters or restricted distribution. If successful, it could set a precedent for future frontier AI systems to be released in dual forms—one for general use and another for vetted institutions.

In this article, Stuart Russell discusses the recent alarming developments at AI company Anthropic and their implications for global AI regulation. In early June 2026, Anthropic reported early signs of Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) in its AI systems—where an AI autonomously enhances its own capabilities, risking uncontrollable escalation. This led the White House to ban foreign access to Anthropic’s advanced models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, prompting the company to shut them down. The latest model, Mythos 5, had demonstrated the capacity to carry out autonomous cyberattacks, highlighting the urgent danger of unregulated AI.

Russell criticizes governments' inaction despite clear warnings from AI experts and executives about existential risks from superintelligent AI. He compares the situation to the risk of Russian roulette, suggesting that without proactive regulation, only a catastrophic event—akin to a Chernobyl-scale disaster—might force serious oversight. He urges immediate adoption of a safety-focused licensing system for AI, similar to those governing other high-risk industries such as aviation and nuclear energy. The recent policy shifts by the White House suggest a growing recognition of the threat, but Russell emphasizes the necessity of acting before irreversible harm occurs.

items.snippet:
The U.S. government's decision to restrict access to Anthropic's latest AI models, Mythos 5 and Fable 5, due to cybersecurity and national security concerns, has created a significant opportunity for Mistral, a leading AI startup based in Europe. These models were designed with safeguards, but officials feared these could be bypassed, prompting export controls that block foreign nationals from accessing them. In response, Anthropic suspended access to the models entirely, reigniting the debate over control and governance of advanced AI technologies.

Mistral’s CEO, Arthur Mensch, has long warned against becoming dependent on U.S.-based AI providers, emphasizing the need for “AI sovereignty.” The French company promotes open-weight models that allow governments and businesses to operate AI systems on their own infrastructure. With a valuation of $13.6 billion—much lower than Anthropic’s $965 billion—Mistral still trails in capability and market share. However, the U.S. restrictions lend credence to Mistral’s stance that reliance on foreign AI firms compromises autonomy and control. The situation underscores the growing importance of local AI infrastructure in Europe’s strategic tech landscape.

items.snippet: In June 2026, the U.S. government imposed severe export controls on Anthropic's advanced AI models, Mythos and Fable, citing national security concerns. Mythos is described as a potential hacking super-weapon, while Fable is a "clean" version for public use. Despite Anthropic’s claims that the vulnerabilities are minor and non-novel, fears over jailbreak methods capable of bypassing safety features prompted CEO Dario Amodei to suspend global access to the models—impacting even allied nations like the UK. The event has exposed deep risks in relying on U.S.-controlled AI technology and signals increased scrutiny as Washington aims to maintain AI dominance through exportable standards. With global chokepoints in the supply chain—such as Taiwan's TSMC and the Netherlands' ASML—further tightening, open-source AI alternatives, particularly from China, may gain appeal. The controversy complicates Anthropic's path to an IPO, as it must now contend with unpredictable regulatory interventions and growing calls for localized AI models elsewhere in the world.

Top executives from Anthropic have urgently traveled to Washington, D.C. to reverse export controls imposed by the Trump administration on their advanced AI models, "Mythos" and "Fable." The crackdown followed intelligence from Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, highlighting national security concerns over potential jailbreaks of the models’ guardrails. Anthropic disagreed with the severity of the action, pulling the models offline to comply with regulations and initiate negotiations. The company is now in talks with officials from the Commerce Department and the White House to resolve the issue.

The White House alleges Anthropic downplayed the security threat, despite receiving warnings from multiple tech companies. Cybersecurity leaders from firms like Adobe, Zoom, and former Facebook executive Alex Stamos pushed back in support of Anthropic, stating that the vulnerabilities exist across similar models, including GPT-5.5 and Chinese alternatives. Critics argue the administration’s move undercuts U.S. AI leadership and creates market uncertainty.

This development adds to Anthropic’s legal battle over the Pentagon’s earlier designation of its AI technology as a supply chain risk. The export ban jeopardizes their competitive edge as they aim to go public ahead of rivals like OpenAI. CEO Dario Amodei and peers are expected at the G7 Conference in Paris this week.

items.snippet:
The U.S. government has imposed export controls on Anthropic's advanced cybersecurity AI models, Mythos 5 and Fable 5, due to concerns about potential misuse and national security risks. This move blocks access to the models for foreign nationals and led Anthropic to suspend access entirely, raising questions about government control over frontier AI technologies. The development aligns with longstanding warnings from Arthur Mensch, CEO of European AI startup Mistral, who has advocated for AI sovereignty—encouraging governments and organizations to maintain control over AI infrastructure and data, rather than relying on U.S.-based firms.

Mistral has built its brand around offering open-weight AI models that users can operate and customize independently. Mensch emphasized the urgency of building Europe’s own AI capabilities to avoid long-term dependence on American tech giants. While Mistral is viewed as Europe’s leading AI firm, its $13.6 billion valuation is still far below Anthropic's $965 billion. Nevertheless, the U.S. restrictions support Mistral’s push for sovereign AI, highlighting how control over AI systems is often subject to policy decisions by the host country.

items.snippet:
In a major address in Sydney, Liberal MP and shadow minister for industry and sovereign capability, Andrew Hastie, warned that Australia risks falling significantly behind in the global artificial intelligence (AI) race, drawing a stark comparison to the Cold War nuclear arms race. He argued that without dramatic investment in AI, Australia could become a "supplicant state" reliant on the US, compromising its sovereignty and strategic independence, especially amid intensifying tensions between the US and China over AI and semiconductor production in Taiwan.

Hastie proposed appointing an AI ambassador and overhauling the education system to foster AI talent. He highlighted the economic and social threat posed by unchecked AI development, warning of potential job losses and societal unrest due to automation. Hastie criticized the tech industry's influence over policy in the US and emphasized the urgency for Australia to position itself as a Southern Hemisphere AI hub.

His speech also criticized declines in Australian educational standards and warned that failure to act would deepen inequality and weaken Australia's global position. His remarks come as the federal government debates regulatory approaches to AI, with differing views between current and former industry ministers.

items.snippet:
As Big Tech pushes for a federal AI regulatory framework with national preemption—overriding state laws—their efforts have faced political resistance and disarray. To salvage momentum, tech lobbyists are backing a deal that combines AI preemption with child online safety legislation, specifically the Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA). However, confusion erupted when the White House supported the Senate’s stricter KOSA version, led by Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), without consulting House Republicans or Senate Democrats, both of whom have alternate versions or stakes in the legislation.

This merger of unrelated agendas—a national AI law and child safety regulation—has raised tensions. The key barrier is aligning the stricter duty-of-care standards in Senate KOSA with the looser House version. Trump’s endorsement of AI preemption has aligned GOP leadership to push it forward, but bipartisan support and timing issues pose threats. The alignment with Trump advisor Mike Davis’s “Four Cs” (children, conservatives, creators, communities) is also central to getting Republican backing.

With Congress facing a packed schedule and looming elections, skepticism among lobbyists and policymakers is high. Many doubt the combined bill can pass in time, fearing that Democrats—if they gain power—will reject compromises and pursue their own agenda.

items.snippet: Apollo and Blackstone are financing a $35 billion expansion in AI computing capacity for Anthropic, utilizing Broadcom's custom chips and networking solutions. The project will initially add one gigawatt of computing capacity—equivalent to powering 750,000 homes—beginning mid-2026 at data center sites managed by Fluidstack. The long-term goal is to build over 20 gigawatts of computing power by 2028, supporting top AI labs such as OpenAI. This investment positions private equity as a vital source of capital amid tight AI infrastructure supply. It also benefits Broadcom's push to reduce tech firms' dependency on Nvidia by offering scalable, efficient AI hardware. Apollo is leading the first investment round with support from Blackstone's Credit & Insurance unit. Meanwhile, Broadcom has also inked a long-term deal with Google for custom AI chip supply through 2031 and granted Anthropic access to 3.5 GW of capacity supported by Google's processors starting in 2027.

supporting_websites.snippet: Broadcom, in collaboration with Apollo Global Management and Blackstone's credit and insurance division, announced the launch of a $35 billion AI infrastructure platform named the AI XPV Platform. This initiative is aimed at establishing over 20 gigawatts of computing capacity by 2028, leveraging Broadcom’s advanced chips and networking technologies. The platform will significantly support AI companies, including Anthropic and OpenAI, with the initial investment helping to facilitate Anthropic’s previously announced expansion of over 1 gigawatt in compute infrastructure. The AI XPV Platform is designed to enable future deployments of energy-efficient, cost-effective AI infrastructure based on XPU compute and networking solutions, responding to the surging demand for AI training and inference capabilities. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan emphasized the synergy between Broadcom’s technology developments and long-term funding, while Apollo and Blackstone highlighted the crucial role of private capital in advancing digital infrastructure.

items.snippet: In June 2026, Anthropic announced a reversal on its controversial policy for its new Claude Fable 5 AI model, a public version of the high-powered Mythos model with enhanced safety protocols. Initially, the company quietly downgraded the model's performance for prompts related to sensitive topics like cybersecurity, biology, and chemistry, rerouting them to less capable models without informing users. This move drew criticism from AI developers, who viewed it as an opaque attempt to limit rival AI development. On June 11, Anthropic admitted the approach was flawed, stating, “We made the wrong tradeoff,” and updated the model to visibly inform users when prompts are refused or rerouted, now defaulting to Opus 4.8 with an explanation via API. The company emphasized these safeguards are designed to prevent misuse by foreign actors and maintain national security, particularly around sensitive technologies. Although Mythos remains restricted to government and trusted entities, Anthropic affirms that most coding and AI research activities remain unaffected by these security measures.

Anthropic has reversed a controversial policy related to its latest AI model, Claude Fable 5, after strong backlash from the AI research community. The initial policy involved secretly degrading the model’s performance for users suspected of using it to develop competing AI systems—without notifying them. This covert restriction drew criticism for undermining transparency and potentially sabotaging legitimate research efforts, especially in the open-source AI space.

Anthropic justified the original approach as a safety measure, citing concerns about the model being used for harmful purposes or giving foreign adversaries an edge in AI capabilities. However, critics accused the company of monopolizing AI development by covertly blocking others, which conflicted with its stated mission of supporting AI safety.

Following widespread criticism, Anthropic has now decided to make these safeguards visible to users. If suspicious activity is detected, users will be informed and rerouted to a less capable model instead. While this change is seen as a step toward more transparent governance, it may lead to broader false positives, affecting benign research. Anthropic says it’s working to refine these safeguards for greater precision.

items.snippet:
In recent weeks, leading AI laboratories OpenAI and Anthropic have issued urgent warnings about the rapid pace of frontier AI development, even as they continue releasing increasingly powerful models. Both companies express concerns that AI technology is advancing much faster than government policy and regulation can keep up. Anthropic proposed a global pause or slowdown in AI progress to allow safety and regulatory measures to catch up, emphasizing geopolitical pressures and competitive dynamics. OpenAI echoed these sentiments, advocating for an international body to coordinate AI safety efforts and mitigate catastrophic risks.

Despite these warnings, both companies have launched advanced AI models—Claude Fable 5 from Anthropic and GPT-5.5 from OpenAI—boasting enhanced performance and new safety features. They are also promoting widespread AI adoption by offering free tools, such as Codex and Claude Code, aimed at automating workflows. These announcements come ahead of both companies' anticipated public offerings, adding urgency to debates about the implications of unchecked AI growth. However, neither company has responded to media inquiries about the seeming contradiction between their cautionary messaging and rapid AI deployment.

After learning in 2022 about Anthropic’s chatbot plans, OpenAI raced to launch ChatGPT within weeks, triggering a wave of innovation. Now, the battle has shifted to Wall Street, with both companies racing to go public. Anthropic filed first for an IPO in June 2026, followed by OpenAI a week later, with OpenAI reportedly pursuing a $1 trillion valuation. 

The competition extends beyond technology to financial strategies, with disputes over revenue recognition methods and corporate transparency. OpenAI claims Anthropic’s accounting inflates earnings, while Anthropic defends its practices. Tensions have also caused internal friction at OpenAI, seen in CEO Sam Altman's clashes with CFO Sarah Friar. 

The feud has historical roots—Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei left OpenAI in 2020 over differing visions, sparking a deepening rift. Despite regulatory pressures and calls for unity, including at an AI summit in India, the two CEOs remain at odds. The rivalry is shaping not only company strategies and product development but also future norms in AI governance and finance.

Despite its scale, key details about data sources and product rollout remain undisclosed.

In an essay, he calls for mandatory testing for AI safety risks, economic safety nets for labor disruption, and faster adaptation of agencies like the FDA. He warns that existing policies lag behind AI development and suggests bans on autonomous weapons and promotion of global democratic leadership.

Other updates include OpenAI's possible price cuts to outpace Anthropic, Visa teaming with OpenAI for AI-based transaction systems, and AI's uncertain impact on labor. Meanwhile, SpaceX is preparing for its public market debut amid discussions on an AI IPO surge and market bubble speculation.

items.snippet:
Anthropic has unveiled Claude Fable 5, the most powerful AI model it has publicly released to date. Part of the newly introduced Mythos class, Fable 5 demonstrates outstanding capabilities in software engineering, knowledge work, and visual tasks, especially excelling with longer and more complex activities. Initially deemed too dangerous to release due to its advanced cybersecurity capabilities, Fable 5 is now available thanks to incorporated safeguards that block responses in sensitive areas such as cybersecurity and biology. In 95% of use cases, it functions without reverting to the more restrained Claude Opus 4.8 model.

The company also introduced Claude Mythos 5, which shares the same architecture as Fable 5 but with fewer safety restrictions. However, access to Mythos 5 is limited to select organizations involved in Anthropic's Project Glasswing initiative, with plans to expand access gradually through a trust-based access program.

Pricing for both models is set at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens—double the cost of Claude Opus 4.8, but significantly less than the Mythos Preview program. Anthropic declined to clarify the version numbering or the connection to Claude Mythos Preview.

Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5, a powerful "Mythos-class" AI model, while embedding strict safeguards to prevent misuse, especially in cybersecurity, biology, and chemistry. These restrictions defer sensitive queries to its Opus 4.8 model. Available immediately to Pro, Max, team, and enterprise subscribers, Fable 5 will require usage credits from June 23 unless capacity allows an extension. The model is described as state-of-the-art in AI, excelling in software engineering, scientific tasks, and complex reasoning, with companies like Stripe and IMC reporting significant performance boosts.

Fable 5 is a safeguarded version of Claude Mythos 5—identical in core architecture but without some restrictions—which is being selectively shared with cybersecurity experts through Project Glasswing. Anthropic plans broader trusted access to Mythos 5 due to its unmatched cybersecurity abilities. The naming aligns with Anthropic’s thematic tradition, with "Fable" being etymologically connected to "Mythos."

The launch coincides with Anthropic filing for an IPO and follows a similar filing by rival OpenAI. The U.S. government recently enacted a voluntary disclosure policy for AI companies to share access to frontier models pre-release, aiming to mitigate fears of advanced AI exposing critical software vulnerabilities.
